idiom_name: explicit state loop first, closure-returning steps where the steps must stay separate
implementation_notes: Go has no tail-call elimination, but the runtime grows and shrinks goroutine stacks automatically (a new goroutine starts with a few kilobytes), so deep recursion usually just runs and the pattern is not the default answer. Where depth is genuinely unbounded - or a goroutine stack limit must not be approached - the local idiom is an explicit loop over a small state value; the classic thunk structure survives only when the mutually recursive steps must remain separate functions, in which case each returns a closure of type `func() step` and one loop calls them until nil. Prefer the loop: it is shorter, allocation-free and readable, and the goroutine stack growth covers the depths that made a trampoline necessary elsewhere.
pitfalls: The closure form allocates a closure per step and forces it to escape to the heap; a plain state loop avoids the allocation entirely.

Goroutine stacks grow to a large but finite limit (the runtime aborts on overflow and no recover can catch it), so unbounded recursion is still fatal - the trampoline only removes the depth dependency.
Mutual recursion split across goroutines needs explicit synchronisation of the state hand-off; the trampoline form is single-goroutine by construction.
